Incorporating the November 2021 Beige Book alongside the FOMC statement and SLOOS shifts the tone modestly more positive. The Beige Book reports that economic activity increased across most Federal Reserve Districts in October–November, with stronger consumer spending and rising leisure and hospitality activity. At the same time, supply chain disruptions and labor shortages continued to constrain growth and contributed to elevated price pressures, and light-vehicle sales were held back by limited inventories. These observations align with the FOMC’s acknowledgment of elevated inflation and virus-related risks but also confirm ongoing expansion.

Layered on top of this, the SLOOS shows broad easing in lending standards (RRE, HELOCs, consumer credit, cards, autos, and CRE), increased credit card limits, reduced auto loan rates, and generally firmer loan demand, reinforcing the “accommodative financial conditions” described by the FOMC. Offsetting factors include pockets of softer demand (autos, some C&I) and unchanged standards/demand in certain niches.

Net: improving credit supply and resilient demand, plus broad-based activity gains in the Beige Book, outweigh ongoing constraints and risks, nudging sentiment modestly higher.
